title: Gen. Green Clay, the surveyor who built Clermont
summary: Green Clay came to Kentucky as a young surveyor, took his pay in land until he held more than 40,000 acres, built Clermont in Madison County, and held Fort Meigs in 1813.
bodyMarkdown:
Green Clay crossed the mountains carrying a surveyor’s compass and chain, and the chain made him rich. Born on August 14, 1757, in the part of Virginia that became [Powhatan County](https://grokipedia.com/page/Green_Clay), he learned the trade as an apprentice and was in Kentucky County by 1777. By 1781 he held an appointment as [deputy surveyor of Lincoln County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Clay), Virginia, at a time when overlapping warrants and careless early surveys were seeding lawsuits that would outlast most of the men who filed them.

## Paid in land

Frontier surveyors were often paid with a share of the ground they laid off, and Clay [kept a portion of the land he surveyed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Hall_State_Historic_Site) as his fee. He bought and sold as well, and in time his holdings passed [40,000 acres](https://grokipedia.com/page/Green_Clay), much of it in Madison County, which Virginia formed out of Lincoln County in 1785 and [organized at Milford in 1786](https://history.ky.gov/markers/milford). Land led to business. Clay built distilleries and a tavern and [ran ferries across the Kentucky River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Clay); the crossing still called [Clay’s Ferry](https://grokipedia.com/page/Green_Clay) grew out of that trade.

It also led to office. Madison County sent him to the Virginia House of Delegates and to the [Virginia ratifying convention of 1788](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Clay), where he and fellow delegate John Miller voted for amendments and against ratifying the Constitution without them. After statehood he sat in the Kentucky House and Senate, was a leader at the 1799 constitutional convention, and was chosen speaker of the Senate in 1808. That same year he ran for governor and finished third.

## Clermont

In 1795 Clay married Sally Lewis, and in [1799 he completed Clermont](https://history.ky.gov/markers/white-hall), a Georgian brick house on his Madison County land. Their children included Brutus J. Clay, born in 1808, and [Cassius Marcellus Clay](https://grokipedia.com/page/Cassius_Marcellus_Clay), born in 1810. The plantation ran on the labor of enslaved people. Clay was one of the largest slaveholders in Kentucky and was thought to be among the wealthiest men in the state, and he expressed no public opposition to the system his son Cassius would spend a lifetime attacking.

## Fort Meigs

In the War of 1812 Clay was commissioned a general of Kentucky militia. In the spring of 1813 he led a brigade north to relieve William Henry Harrison, besieged at [Fort Meigs](https://grokipedia.com/page/Siege_of_Fort_Meigs) on the Maumee River in Ohio. On May 5 a detachment under Col. William Dudley landed on the far bank, overran the British batteries and spiked the guns, then chased retreating warriors into the woods and was cut apart; hundreds of Kentuckians were killed, wounded, or captured in what became known as Dudley’s Defeat.

Clay’s own column fought its way into the fort, and when the siege lifted Harrison left him in command.

The British and Tecumseh returned in July. Outside the walls they staged a sham battle meant to look like an attack on an American relief column, hoping to lure the garrison out. Clay [knew no reinforcements were on the way](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Clay), kept his men behind the earthworks, and held the fort until the besiegers gave up and left.

## Kentucky today

Clay died at his Madison County home on October 31, 1828. [Clay County](https://history.ky.gov/markers/county-named-1806-3) carries his name. In the 1860s, while Cassius served as U.S. minister to Russia, his wife Mary Jane Warfield Clay oversaw the remodeling that wrapped Clermont inside the Italianate mansion called White Hall. The house is now [White Hall State Historic Site](https://history.ky.gov/markers/white-hall) near Richmond, where an early portrait of Green Clay still hangs.
